title: Zoning & Sequences of Operation

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Conference table with a printed reflected ceiling plan of an open office and colored markers. Matthew seated. Medium shot.
scenes.says: An NLC system only does what it's told. Zoning decides which luminaires respond together to which input. Get it wrong and the building wastes energy, annoys people, or fails an energy-code test. As a senior tech, you're often the one who notices the zones on paper don't make sense in the real space. Catch it at the planning stage, not after the owner complains.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Senior tech color-codes the plan: blue for control zones, green for occupancy, yellow for daylight. Overhead shot. Presenter voice-over.
scenes.on_screen: Control | Occupancy | Daylight | Scene/group | Emergency group
scenes.says: Zone types. A control zone answers a wallstation or schedule. An occupancy zone is the area a sensor can see reliably. A daylight zone is the area daylight reaches from windows or skylights. Scenes cover task or presentation areas. And the emergency group responds to loss of normal power through a UL 924 device. One fixture is usually in several zones at once. That's normal.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: In the real open office: senior tech stands at the window wall, then walks inward, marking the primary and secondary sidelit bands with tape on the floor.
scenes.says: Daylight zones are defined by the energy code. The primary sidelit zone is the band closest to the windows, roughly one window-head height deep. The secondary is the next band in. Toplit is under and around skylights. Your field job: confirm the fixtures in each zone match the drawings, and that primary and secondary are controlled separately when the code or design requires it.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Matthew reads a printed SOO aloud; text appears on screen.
scenes.on_screen: "Manual-ON to 50%... high-end trim 85%... OFF 15 minutes after vacancy... maintain 30 fc at the desk... after-hours 5-minute grace with warning flash"
scenes.says: The sequence of operations is the written description of how each space behaves. Here's a private office: manual-on to 50 percent, occupant can raise to 100, high-end trim at 85. Vacancy sensor off 15 minutes after vacancy. Daylight dims the primary zone to hold 30 footcandles at the desk. After hours, a 5-minute grace period with a warning flash before shutoff.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Split screen: SOO line on the left, matching software setting on a tablet on the right, one row at a time.
scenes.on_screen: Manual-ON 50% = vacancy mode + ON level 50% | 85% trim = max output 85% | 15 min = timeout | 30 fc = meter-calibrated setpoint
scenes.says: Now break every phrase into a setting. Manual-on to 50 percent: sensor mode vacancy, wallstation on level 50. High-end trim 85: maximum output 85. Off 15 minutes after vacancy: timeout 15. Thirty footcandles at the desk: daylight setpoint calibrated with a meter at the desk. Grace period: a schedule event, flash-warn and override duration. If a phrase won't translate, or two conflict, raise it before you program.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Walking the space: an L-shaped room with one sensor; a conference room sensor with a view into the hallway; a break room on the open-office zone.
scenes.on_screen: Coverage gaps | Seeing through doors | Daylight sensor seeing electric light | Mixed space types
scenes.says: Mistakes to catch. Coverage gaps: one sensor in an L-shaped room misses the far leg. If people wave their arms to turn lights on, that's bad zoning, not a bad sensor. A conference room sensor that sees hallway traffic keeps the room lit all day. A daylight sensor fooled by its own fixtures. And a break room on the open-office zone keeps the whole office on.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Close-up of an exit-path luminaire and a UL 924 device label.
scenes.on_screen: Never rezone or bypass emergency lighting without engineering direction
scenes.says: The serious one: emergency luminaires on regular zones without a UL 924 device. Egress lights could be dimmed or off during a power failure. That's a life-safety deficiency. Never reprogram, rezone or bypass emergency luminaires to fix a controls issue without the design engineer's direction and a documented test afterward.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Tablet screen showing device names like L2-210-LUM-03 and L2-210-OCC-01, one still showing a factory default name highlighted in red.
scenes.on_screen: L2-210-LUM-03 | L2-210-OCC-01 | No factory default names
scenes.says: Finally, naming. On a big project you might name thousands of devices. Use the project's convention exactly. A good one encodes floor, room, device type and position, like L2-210-LUM-03. It makes troubleshooting, BMS mapping and rezoning far easier. Never leave a device with its factory default name. Now read the lesson and take the quiz.

production_notes: Printed reflected ceiling plan of a generic open office, colored markers; real open office with windows for the daylight-zone walk (tape on the floor for zone bands); tablet showing a generic NLC app with SOO-to-setting mapping (mock screens, no vendor branding). Senior tech does the marker and walk segments while Matthew narrates. Knowledge/planning lesson: hook connects zoning to planned work instead of a full Job Mindset opener.
